title: VaultCreated event filter trusts any package whose tx-module is 'tpsl_vault'
description: discoverVaultsTick uses a MoveModule filter (`package: tpslVaultPackageId, module: 'tpsl_vault'`) which per Cycle 1 friction-log selects on the EMITTING transactionModule, not the event-defining package. The post-RPC type guard `raw.type?.endsWith('::tpsl_vault::VaultCreated')` is a string-suffix check that does NOT bind the type to the configured tpslVaultPackageId. Any attacker who publishes their own package containing a module named `tpsl_vault` and an event type whose name ends with `::tpsl_vault::VaultCreated` and emits it from a tx whose transactionModule is `tpsl_vault` could in principle have events surfaced through the RPC filter (the filter package binding constrains the emitting package, but neither layer cross-checks `raw.packageId === tpslVaultPackageId`). The keeper would then parse the foreign payload, insert a bogus KnownVault into the registry, and attempt to fire `execute_trigger` against attacker-controlled vault_id / pool_id values.
impact: Registry poisoning. The keeper would burn DEEP fees attempting triggers on bogus vault IDs, log misleading `vault_discovered` lines that confuse operators, and (if the attacker's pool_id resolves to a real DeepBook pool) potentially execute swaps the operator did not authorize. On localnet the blast radius is small, but this is an exploit class that should be closed before any move beyond localnet.
recommendation: Add an explicit `raw.packageId === tpslVaultPackageId` (and full type prefix check `raw.type === "${tpslVaultPackageId}::tpsl_vault::VaultCreated"` after address-normalization) gate inside the loop in src/index.ts:253. Alternatively switch the RPC filter to `MoveEventType` with the fully-qualified type — the contract explicitly permits this and it removes the ambiguity.

title: Manifest path is read without integrity validation; SANDBOX_MANIFEST_PATH overrideable
description: main() reads the deployment manifest with `fs.readFileSync(config.sandboxManifestPath, 'utf-8')` then `JSON.parse`s it, with no schema validation beyond TypeScript's structural typing (which is erased at runtime). The path is overridable via SANDBOX_MANIFEST_PATH. A maliciously crafted manifest could redirect `network.rpcUrl` to a hostile node (causing the keeper to leak its address, accept fabricated price/event responses, and submit signed trigger transactions to the attacker's relay) or substitute `pythOracles.{deep,sui}PriceInfoObjectId` with attacker-controlled object IDs (combined with an attacker-controlled rpcUrl this enables full price spoofing). The contract explicitly disclaims schema validation as out-of-scope ("The keeper does not validate manifest schema beyond the field presence checks"), so this is documented behavior — but the file-existence check at startup is the only barrier.
impact: On localnet (the sole supported deployment per spec) this is bounded by filesystem trust; if SANDBOX_MANIFEST_PATH is ever set from an untrusted source, the keeper becomes a trivial signing oracle for arbitrary devInspect-shaped requests.
recommendation: Document the trust boundary explicitly in the keeper's RUNBOOK (the manifest path and its contents are part of the keeper's trusted base). For defense-in-depth, validate that `network.rpcUrl` matches `http://127.0.0.1:9000` (the documented localnet endpoint) and that all 0x-prefixed IDs in the manifest pass the same hex regex used in config.ts.
evidence:
const manifestRaw = fs.readFileSync(config.sandboxManifestPath, 'utf-8');
const manifest = JSON.parse(manifestRaw) as SandboxManifest;

title: Pyth-trust model is load-bearing and undocumented in keeper source
description: The keeper supplies `current_price: u64` to `tpsl_vault::execute_trigger`, and per Cycle 3 review the Move contract's only protection against a wrong price is the TP/SL gate itself (the contract trusts the keeper for the price value). This means the keeper is a fully privileged price oracle from the Move contract's perspective: a compromised keeper key, a manifest-tampering attacker (R6-002), or even a logic bug in the keeper's price computation (see R6-005 re: hardcoded quoteDecimals=9) directly translates to vaults firing at the wrong on-chain price, with the residual / quote routed to the vault owner regardless of whether the price was ever real. This trust assumption is intentional per spec but is not flagged anywhere in the keeper sources or notes/pyth-shape.md.
impact: Operators reading the keeper code in isolation may assume the on-chain Move contract validates the price. Future cycles or external integrators inheriting this code could miss the implicit trust requirement.
recommendation: Add a one-line module-comment at the top of triggerSubmitter.ts (and/or in notes/pyth-shape.md) stating: "The Move contract trusts the keeper-supplied current_price; the keeper is the price oracle from the contract's perspective. Compromised keeper key or manifest = compromised price." This is documentation, not code.

title: Keeper restart re-fires already-triggered vaults — seedTriggeredFromChain defined but unused
description: VaultRegistry.seedTriggeredFromChain (vaultRegistry.ts:160) is defined per contract decision #3 to re-seed the in-memory `triggered` flag from on-chain state at boot. However, main() in index.ts never calls it. After a keeper restart, the in-memory cache shows `triggered: false` for every rediscovered vault; on the first poll cycle that satisfies the TP/SL condition the keeper will attempt to fire `execute_trigger` against every already-fired vault. The on-chain Move contract's `EVaultTriggered` assertion blocks the actual execution (defense-in-depth), so funds are not at risk, but every retried vault costs the keeper a wasted gas+DEEP submission and pollutes the structured log with `trigger_failed` entries that operators must triage.
impact: DoS against the keeper's own DEEP balance and gas budget on restart; noise in the logs that the Cycle 5 UI / E-007 harness will see as spurious failures.
recommendation: In main() between the registry construction and the poll loop, after the first discoverVaultsTick fills the registry, await Promise.all([...registry.iterate()].map(v => registry.seedTriggeredFromChain(v.vault_id, getObjectFn))) using a small JSON-RPC wrapper for sui_getObject. The implementation cost is ~10 lines.

title: Hardcoded quoteDecimals=9 in production poll cycle widens price-spoofing surface
description: runOnePollCycle computes current_price with `quoteDecimals: 9` hardcoded, with the comment "Default SUI decimals; manifest-driven in production". This is the production poll cycle (main() calls runOnePollCycle directly), not a test path. For any vault whose pool's quote coin is not SUI (e.g., the SUI/USDC pool which the contract explicitly mentions in section 1 of behavior), the formula returns a current_price off by 10^3 (USDC=6 vs SUI=9 hardcoded). Combined with the Pyth-trust model (R6-003), this means the keeper will fire triggers at consistently-wrong prices for every non-SUI-quote pool, with no on-chain check.
impact: User funds in non-SUI-quote vaults swap at incorrect price thresholds. From a security lens: any attacker who can predict the off-by-1000 in either direction can trade against the swap to extract value, knowing the keeper will fire 1000x earlier or later than the user intended. This is a real economic exploit vector against real user funds, even if the localnet scope keeps real-world impact bounded.
recommendation: Resolve the vault's pool_id against manifest.pools[*] at vault discovery time, store baseDecimals/quoteDecimals on the KnownVault record, and pass the per-vault quoteDecimals into calculateBaseQuotePrice. The KnownVault interface already has slots for baseCoinType/quoteCoinType (vaultRegistry.ts:44-46); extend the same pattern for decimals.
evidence: quoteDecimals: 9, // Default SUI decimals; manifest-driven in production

title: Logger redaction list misses ed25519 SDK 2.x getter and PrivateKey export shapes
description: SECRET_KEYS = new Set(['secretKey', 'privateKey', 'seed']) is the redaction allow-list. Sui SDK 2.x Ed25519Keypair exposes the secret via `getSecretKey()` (returns a `suiprivkey1...` bech32 string) and `export()` (returns `{ schema, privateKey }`). The redaction key for the bech32 export is the function name `getSecretKey`, not a field name, so it cannot be redacted by key-name match if a developer ever does `logger.info('debug', { keypair })` or spreads the keypair object. Additionally, the logger only inspects top-level keys — nested `{ wallet: { privateKey: '...' } }` would leak. The spec.md `never logged in full` rule treats the logger as a defense-in-depth layer; the Set is the entire defense.
impact: Defense-in-depth weakening. The current code path doesn't pass the keypair to the logger anywhere (verified by grep), so this is dormant; but a future change that does so would silently leak the secret key. There is no test that asserts a keypair-shaped object cannot be logged.
recommendation: Add `getSecretKey`, `secret`, `mnemonic`, `entropy` to the redaction set; recurse one level for object values so nested secret-shaped keys are also dropped; add a vitest case in logger.test.ts that constructs a synthetic keypair-shaped object and asserts no `suiprivkey1` substring leaks into stdout.

title: SIGINT/SIGTERM handler exits immediately without draining in-flight transactions
description: Contract Behavior > Lifecycle says the keeper installs SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers that "stop the two loops, drain in-flight transactions, log a `keeper_shutdown` line, and exit zero". The implementation logs the line and immediately calls process.exit(0) inside the handler, with no await on any in-flight `signAndSubmitTrigger` (in fairness, no submission is wired in at all — see R6-008 — but the lifecycle behavior is still wrong). If a trigger is mid-submission when the signal lands, the in-flight HTTP request to sui_executeTransactionBlock continues on the Sui side and the tx may land on-chain after the keeper has already logged shutdown.
impact: Operators reading logs cannot rely on `keeper_shutdown` being the truthful last line of behavior — a `trigger_fired` may yet land on-chain after shutdown is logged. This is a low-severity audit-trail issue rather than a fund-loss issue.
recommendation: Track in-flight trigger promises in a Set; in the shutdown handler, set running=false, await Promise.allSettled(inFlight) with a 5s timeout, then emit keeper_shutdown and exit. Since trigger submission is not wired at all today (R6-008), the simpler immediate fix is to just call process.exit(0) at the END of the next loop iteration (after the loop sees running=false), instead of from inside the signal handler.

title: Production poll loop never invokes signAndSubmitTrigger — keeper logs intent but never fires
description: runOnePollCycle is the function the production main() calls. Its trigger-evaluation loop emits logTriggerAttempt and then exits with the comment `// Note: trigger submission requires a signer, which is only available in the full boot path. In runOnePollCycle (test seam), we skip submission.` However, main() has no separate code path that invokes buildTriggerTransaction / signAndSubmitTrigger after runOnePollCycle returns; the keypair generated in main() is never threaded into the poll cycle. From a security lens this is a silent failure mode: the keeper convinces operators (via the structured log stream the Cycle 5 UI / E-007 harness consumes) that conditions were evaluated and triggers attempted, but no on-chain transaction is ever submitted, so vault owners' TP/SL orders silently never fire.
impact: User funds locked in vaults will never be realized at the configured TP/SL prices. The Move contract's correctness is irrelevant — the keeper, the only off-chain agent that calls execute_trigger, never calls it. Worse, the log stream is positively misleading: a `trigger_attempt` line strongly implies a submission attempt followed.
recommendation: Refactor so the signer is an injectable dependency on PollCycleArgs (matching the contract's spec for index.ts decomposition); main() constructs the signer once and passes it. After logTriggerAttempt, call buildTriggerTransaction + signAndSubmitTrigger and emit logTriggerFired/logTriggerFailed with the result. The rename of the comment `(test seam)` to `(production path)` is a tell — the green-phase synthesis stopped at the seam without finishing the production wiring.
evidence:
// Note: trigger submission requires a signer, which is only available
// in the full boot path. In runOnePollCycle (test seam), we skip submission.

title: tx.build({ client: undefined as never }) will throw on shared-object refs at runtime
description: signAndSubmitTrigger calls `tx.build({ client: undefined as never })`. Vault and Pool are SHARED objects per the contract; the Sui SDK 2.x Transaction.build path requires a client to fetch each shared object's initial_shared_version when building. Passing undefined coerced through `as never` silences the TypeScript type system but does not change the runtime requirement. When (if) this code path is reached (it currently isn't — see R6-008), it will throw before producing tx bytes, leaving the signer unused. From a security lens, the unreachable failure path is a defense-in-depth blocker against accidentally-firing triggers, but it also means there is no live test that the signing/submission shape is correct end-to-end.
impact: If R6-008 is fixed without also fixing this, the first production trigger attempt will throw inside build() and surface as a generic poll cycle error, not a structured trigger_failed log line. The log stream the harness consumes will be less informative than spec'd.
recommendation: Construct a SuiJsonRpcClient in main() (per the SDK 2.0 docs the implementer is required to read), inject it into buildTriggerTransaction so shared-object initial versions are resolved, and remove the `as never` cast. Alternatively, do an explicit sui_getObject for vaultId and poolId before build() and pass `tx.sharedObjectRef({ objectId, mutable: true, initialSharedVersion })` instead of `tx.object(...)` (the contract's Implementation guidance > Shared-object handling section explicitly documents this fallback).
evidence: const txBytes = await tx.build({ client: undefined as never });
